To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the cationic radi of metals are derived by assuming that the extreme compression of metals results in direct contacts between cationic cores, and that the cation of a binary compound is the sum of the covalent radii of the cation and anion.

the cationic radi of metals are derived by assuming that extreme compression leads to direct contact between atomic cores, that heteronuclear distances in compressed binary compounds are equal to the cationic r of the metal + the covalent r of the nonmetal, and that the r of the cation in an ionic solid is derived by assuming that the cation and the anion are in contact in the extreme compression limit.
the compressibility of a solid can be used to determine the cationic radi of metals, and that the cationic and anionic radii can be used to predict the structure of binary compounds.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new materials and processes for the synthesis of new compounds.
the development of new methods for the preparation of metal nanoparticles and their characterization, with the aim of understanding the fundamental properties of the metal nanoparticles.
the structure, properties, and reactions of the main group elements and their derivatives.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the ionic radii of the metals are not the radii of the ions in a crystal, but the radii of atoms in an extremely compressed metal.
the cations of metals are not spherical and that the cationic radi of metals are not constant.
the radii of cations in extremely compressed solids are smaller than the ionic radii of the same cations in the corresponding crystals.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
cations of all elements are smaller than the corresponding atoms.
the cationic radiis of metals are smaller than the ionic radiis and that the cation size is not affected by the oxidation state.

the cationic radiis are smaller than those derived from ionic crystals, and that the covalent radii are smaller than those obtained by extrapolation of the bond lengths in molecules to zero bond length.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the cationic radiiums of the metals can be derived from the compressibilities of solids assuming that the extreme compression of a metal results in the direct contact between cations (=atomic cores).
the radii of metals in solids are larger than the radii of free atoms.
